source.title: Understanding diffusion models requires rethinking (again) generalization

page_placements.theme: Diffusion memorization, fidelity and limits of benign interpolation

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training-time double descent using test-set FID and sliced Wasserstein distance in diffusion models, rather than supervised prediction error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a double descent in distributional distances and explicit effects of dataset and model size on memorization and peak fidelity. It does not report supervised test-error curves or test error near an interpolation threshold. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The only double-descent-like result is a fall-rise-fall in FID and sliced Wasserstein distance of diffusion-model samples over training steps. These are distributional sample-quality distances, not test error. The curve is the same against the train and test splits, and the authors say this rules out classical double descent and attribute it to optimization dynamics. That is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V2. The model-size and dataset-size sweeps report memorization timing and peak fidelity, not test-error curves.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors attribute the distributional-distance double descent to optimization dynamics. They also say its mechanism is open, and that it was absent in ImageNet experiments. They further argue the memorization question is largely solved by early stopping plus linear scaling of memorization time with N.
record.recipe_differences: Uses rectified-flow diffusion models on CIFAR-10 and tracks memorization and distributional distances, rather than testing supervised prediction error in the original double-descent settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset size delays memorization and improves peak fidelity; model size advances memorization onset and improves peak fidelity. Smaller batch sizes and larger learning rates improve peak fidelity; learning rate also changes normalized memorization timing.

fits_no_version.finding: Rectified-flow U-Net on CIFAR-10 (N=2048, P=92M) shows a fall-rise-fall in FID and sliced Wasserstein distance over training steps. The curves are identical against train and test splits. A per-noise-level loss decomposition showed no pattern explaining it, and it was not observed on ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diffusion models can show an optimization-driven, train/test-symmetric double descent in distributional distance during training, distinct from classical double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger datasets delay memorization and improve peak fidelity. Larger models advance memorization onset but also improve peak fidelity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In diffusion models, dataset size and model size play different roles in memorization timing while both improve fidelity.

record.problems: The authors note that it is unclear whether findings from this intermediate-scale CIFAR-10 study scale to larger models and datasets. The double-descent curves are presented in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. Their test-split measures are distributional distances, not supervised test error.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Hyperparameter effects on peak fidelity are discussed in Sections 3.4 and 4.1 but do not measure a claim version's test-error or peak mechanism.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over model size. The size sweep reports memorization onset and peak fidelity only.
No supervised test-error curve over epochs. Only distributional distances over steps, identical for train and test.
Dataset size is varied, but larger N only improves fidelity. No test error near an interpolation threshold.
No cross-model-class capacity sweep past interpolation.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
No label-noise, multiple-peak or tuned-regularization analysis.

missing.what: States the distributional-distance double descent was not observed in similar ImageNet experiments.
missing.locator: Section 3.2, end of 'Double descent in distributional distance' paragraph
missing.versions: none (would bear on V2 scope if test FID were accepted as test error)

missing.what: Negative test of the noise-level learning-speed hypothesis via loss decomposition; no meaningful pattern found.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline call. If test-split FID is accepted as a generative analogue of test error, r1 and r2 could link to V2 as T3. In that case the verdict would be limits_scope: train and test curves are identical, the pattern is not seen on ImageNet, and the authors deny a generalization-gap origin. The reader's 'supports' label overstates the bearing either way. The study is a position paper with figure-only results and no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size sweep reports memorization timing and peak fidelity, not a fall-rise-fall curve in test error.
The paper reports training-step curves for test-set distributional distances, not supervised prediction error or an epoch-based sweep.
Dataset size is varied, but the paper does not test whether increasing samples raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The paper does not test risk as capacity crosses an interpolation point across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak location.
The paper does not test label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
The paper does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters.
